SHROOMS.name: Grey oyster
SHROOMS.sub: Paddy straw, chopped 3–5 cm. Free around Talcher after harvest.
SHROOMS.yield: 600 g – 1 kg fresh per kg of dry straw
SHROOMS.spawnat: ₹40–80 a bottle at KVK Angul or OUAT
SHROOMS.eat: The everyday one. Meaty, holds up in a besara or a dry fry.
SHROOMS.why: The most forgiving mushroom there is, and the widest temperature band of the oysters. This is the one to learn on.
steps: Chop straw to 3–5 cm. Soak 8–16 hours in clean water.
Pasteurise: 80°C for 45–60 minutes, or steam an hour. A drum on a gas ring is enough.
Drain. Squeeze test — a hard squeeze gives drops, not a stream. That is 65–70%.
Cool to room temperature. Hot straw kills spawn, and this is the commonest beginner mistake.
Fill a 12×18" PP bag in 4–5 layers, spawn around the inner edge of each layer.
Punch 15–20 pinholes, tie off, write the date on the bag.
Dark cupboard, 16–20 days. No water, no opening, no peeking past a glance.
Solid white? Onto a tray on the bottom shelf. Slash the bag in 6–8 places.
Wet the tiles around it twice daily. Crack a window 20 minutes, twice daily.
Harvest by twisting off the whole cluster as the cap edge begins to flatten.
Rest a week, soak the block 20 minutes, drain, repeat for flush two and three.
watch: Long thin stems and tiny caps means not enough fresh air. Open the window more, not less.
Green powder is Trichoderma. Bag it, bin it outside, wash your hands. Never cut it out.
Sour or ammonia smell is bacterial. Discard the bag.

SHROOMS.name: White oyster
SHROOMS.sub: Paddy straw. Same preparation as grey.
SHROOMS.spawnat: ₹40–80 a bottle, same sources as grey
SHROOMS.eat: Softer and whiter than grey. Better in a light curry than a fry.
SHROOMS.why: Slightly narrower band than grey and it wants a touch cooler. December and January in your room are its months.
steps: Identical to grey oyster in every step.
The one difference: it sulks above 30°C, so keep it to the December–February window.
Give it the bottom shelf, which is the coolest place in the room.
watch: Fruits later than grey if the room is warm. Patience, not more water.

SHROOMS.name: Pink oyster
SHROOMS.sub: Paddy straw, sawdust, even cardboard. Aggressive on almost anything.
SHROOMS.first: 14–18 days — the fastest of the lot
SHROOMS.yield: 400–700 g per kg dry straw. Short, sharp run.
SHROOMS.spawnat: Harder to find locally — ask OUAT, or order by post
SHROOMS.eat: Bacon-ish when fried hard. Loses the pink in the pan. Eat within a day.
SHROOMS.why: Colonises so fast it beats contaminants, which makes it the one species you can attempt without proper pasteurisation. But read the warning before you put one in a closed room.
steps: Soak straw overnight. Hot-water treatment is enough; full pasteurisation optional.
Spawn heavily — 4–5%. Speed is the whole strategy with this one.
Bag and hole as for grey oyster.
Colonises in 10–14 days at your temperatures.
Slash and fruit. Pins appear within 3–4 days of opening.
Harvest EARLY, while the caps are still curled under. It goes over in a day.
watch: Heavy spore load. Pink oyster throws far more spores than grey, and in a closed room with one door that means breathing them. Harvest before the caps flatten, wear a mask when handling, and air the room hard. If anyone in the house is asthmatic, skip this species entirely.
Goes slimy and sour fast in the fridge. It is a same-day mushroom.

SHROOMS.name: Golden oyster
SHROOMS.sub: Straw or hardwood sawdust. Prefers sawdust.
SHROOMS.yield: 300–600 g per kg dry substrate. Modest.
SHROOMS.spawnat: Speciality suppliers, rarely at KVK. Order online.
SHROOMS.eat: Cashew-like, delicate, and it shrinks to nothing. Grown for looks and novelty.
SHROOMS.why: Beautiful and it likes your shoulder seasons, but it wants humidity above 90% — which in an enclosed room means a tent, not just a wet floor.
steps: Sawdust substrate gives better results than straw. Supplement with 10% wheat bran.
Sterilise rather than pasteurise if you use sawdust — a pressure cooker, 90 minutes.
Colonise 18–24 days in the dark.
Fruit inside a clear polythene tent to hold 90% humidity. A wet floor alone will not do it.
Harvest the whole bouquet at once, young.
watch: Very fragile. Bruises brown if you handle it twice.
Also a heavy sporer. Same mask advice as pink.

SHROOMS.name: Blue / tree oyster
SHROOMS.yield: 700 g – 1 kg per kg dry straw when it gets its temperature
SHROOMS.spawnat: Commonly sold as plain "oyster" — check which species you are buying
SHROOMS.why: Wants a genuine cool spell. Your December and January nights reach it; the days do not. A one-bag December gamble, not a staple.
steps: Prepare as for grey oyster.
Spawn in late November so the run finishes as January arrives.
Fruit on the floor-level shelf, at night, with the window open. Cold shock triggers pinning.
If February turns warm early, expect it to abort. That is the risk you accepted.
watch: Aborted pins that shrivel and yellow mean it got too warm. Nothing to fix mid-run.

SHROOMS.name: Milky mushroom
SHROOMS.casing: Required. 2–3 cm of clay-loam or cocopeat + garden soil, pasteurised.
SHROOMS.yield: 50–100% of dry substrate weight. Heavy, meaty crop.
SHROOMS.spawnat: OUAT Bhubaneswar carries it. KVK Angul sometimes.
SHROOMS.eat: Thick, white, scallop-like. Keeps 2–3 days at room temperature — the only one that does.
SHROOMS.why: India's own hot-weather mushroom, and the answer to the gap when nothing else will fruit. Genuinely suited to your monsoon room.
steps: Chop and soak straw overnight. Pasteurise at 80°C for an hour.
Drain to 65–70% moisture. Cool.
Fill polythene bags 15×30 cm, spawning in layers at 4–6%.
Spawn run 20–28 days at 30–35°C. Your July cupboard does this without help.
When fully white, open the bag and lay a 2–3 cm casing layer on top. This step is not optional — no casing, no mushrooms.
Casing must be pasteurised: bake it, steam it, or pour boiling water through it.
Keep the casing damp with a fine spray. Never let it dry, never flood it.
Pins appear through the casing in 8–12 days. Harvest when the cap opens flat.
Second flush follows 12–15 days later.
watch: White powdery patches on the casing are plaster mould, from unpasteurised casing soil. Prevention only — there is no cure mid-crop.
Below 25°C it stalls; below 15°C the mycelium dies. Do not attempt in winter.
Needs diffused light to fruit — not darkness, and not your south window either.

SHROOMS.name: Paddy straw mushroom
SHROOMS.sub: Whole paddy straw in bundles, not chopped.
SHROOMS.rate: Spawn 10 cm in from the edge of each layer, with a pinch of gram flour
SHROOMS.first: 10–15 days — fastest crop in the book
SHROOMS.yield: 10–20% of dry straw weight. Grown for speed and flavour, not volume.
SHROOMS.spawnat: ₹40/kg in Bhubaneswar. Locally the best-known mushroom in Odisha.
SHROOMS.eat: The one you already know. Best fresh, same day. Never refrigerate below 15°C — it blackens.
SHROOMS.why: The traditional Odisha monsoon crop, and you already have the straw bundle in the corner. July and August do the humidity for free.
steps: Bundles of 1.5–2 kg, roughly a forearm long. Soak 12–18 hours.
Drain on a slope an hour or two.
Bed on a raised platform or crate — never straight on your tiles.
Stack 4 layers, each turned 90° to the one below.
Spawn 10 cm in from each layer's edge, with a pinch of red or black gram flour.
Cover loosely with clear polythene to hold heat and moisture.
Lift the cover daily for air. Do not soak the bed.
Pinheads by day 8–10. Harvest at button stage while still a firm ball.
watch: Safety, and this one matters. A young paddy-straw button looks very like a young deadly Amanita. Only ever eat what you grew yourself, from bought spawn, in your own bed. Never eat a wild lookalike, and never let anyone else identify it for you.
Once the veil tears the quality collapses. Harvest early or not at all.
That bundle in your corner: get it off the floor and keep it dry until you use it. Damp straw on tiles grows the wrong things.

SHROOMS.name: Wood ear
SHROOMS.sub: Hardwood sawdust bags, or sal/mango logs.
SHROOMS.yield: Low fresh weight, but it dries to a fifth and keeps for a year.
SHROOMS.spawnat: Uncommon in Odisha. Try DMR Solan by post.
SHROOMS.eat: No flavour of its own, all texture. Dries and rehydrates perfectly.
SHROOMS.why: Tolerates your heat and humidity better than any oyster, and dried wood ear stores indefinitely — which suits a room you cannot cool.
steps: Sawdust plus 20% bran, sterilised 90 minutes in a pressure cooker.
Colonise 30–40 days. Slower than oyster — do not panic at week three.
Slash and fruit at 85%+ humidity. Tent it.
Harvest when the ear is fully expanded and rubbery, before it goes translucent.
Sun-dry on a mesh tray. Your March sun does this in a day.
watch: Slow enough that contamination has time to find it. Cleanliness matters more here than with oyster.

SHROOMS.name: Reishi
SHROOMS.yield: One or two conks per bag. Not food by weight.
SHROOMS.spawnat: Speciality only. DMR Solan, or online culture suppliers.
SHROOMS.eat: Not eaten — too woody. Sliced and simmered as a bitter tea.
SHROOMS.why: Takes more heat than any food species here, so it holds the monsoon and the shoulder months when the oysters are marginal. Not the peak of summer though — nothing survives a 50°C May.
steps: Sterilised hardwood sawdust, 20% bran. Pressure cook 2 hours.
Colonise 30–45 days at 28–30°C — July and August do this unaided.
Open the bag partially. It fruits toward light and air — antler form in low air, conk form in higher.
Very slow. Expect 6–10 weeks of visible growth.
Harvest when the white growing edge finally turns red-brown.
Slice thin while fresh, then dry. It becomes rock hard.
watch: Throws a fine rust-red spore dust over everything nearby in the final weeks. Not something to fruit next to your plants or your bed.
The longest commitment on this list. Do not make it your first bag.

SHROOMS.name: Button mushroom
SHROOMS.sub: Composted wheat straw with manure — a three-week fermentation before you even start.
SHROOMS.why: Fruits at 15–18°C. Your room touches that for a few January nights and never for a whole crop. It also needs composted manure, which you cannot make in an enclosed utility room without the smell taking over the flat. This is a cooled-shed crop, not a home one.

SHROOMS.name: Shiitake
SHROOMS.eat: Deep, savoury, the best of the cultivated mushrooms.
SHROOMS.why: Needs 12–20°C to fruit and a 60–90 day colonisation before that. Grown commercially in Himachal and the north-east, not the Odisha plains. Without a cooled room it will colonise and then simply never pin.

SHROOMS.name: King oyster
SHROOMS.eat: Thick stem, scallop texture. The one worth wanting.
SHROOMS.why: Despite the name it is nothing like the other oysters. It fruits at 15–18°C and aborts above 20. Not possible here without refrigeration.

SHROOMS.name: Lion's mane
SHROOMS.why: The closest of the "no" list to possible — a cold January might just hold 18–22°C at night. But it needs that steadily for three weeks, and your daytime highs break it. Attempt only if you ever get a cooled cupboard.

SHROOMS.name: Enoki
SHROOMS.eat: Thin white bundles, mild, for soups.
SHROOMS.why: Fruits at 8–15°C in bottles with a collar to force the long stems. Angul's record low is 4.5°C and its January average low is 8.4 — outdoors, for a few hours, once a year. There is no version of this that works in your room.

oyster: Dark cupboard, no water, no opening. It should go solid white.
Fully white? Onto a tray on the bottom shelf, slash the bag, wet the floor daily.
Slash the bag and move it to the shelf
Pinheads forming. Wet the tiles twice a day, crack a window twice a day.
Wet the floor and air the room
Twist off the whole cluster as the cap edge starts to flatten.
Rest a week, soak the block briefly, repeat.
Soak the block for flush two
Two or three flushes is the run. Compost it.
pink: Fast. It should be visibly running within four days.
Slash it. Pins follow within three or four days.
Wet the floor twice daily. Mask on when you handle it.
While the caps are still curled under. It goes over in a day.
7–10 days after the first. Then it is done.
Short run by design. Compost it.
milky: Fully white? Lay 2–3 cm of pasteurised casing on top. No casing, no mushrooms.
Fine spray only. Never dry, never flooded. Diffused light now.
Pins push through the casing. Do not spray directly onto them.
Cap opened flat. Twist and lift, then patch the casing hole.
Two flushes is the crop. Clear it.
paddy: Cover loosely with polythene. Lift the cover daily for air.
Day 8–10. Do not soak the bed.
Button stage, still a firm ball. Once the veil tears, quality collapses.
Fast and short. Clear the bed.
reishi: Partially open the bag. It fruits toward light and air.
White fingers forming. Weeks of this. Do not intervene.
The white growing edge turns red-brown. Nearly there.
Slice thin while fresh, then dry. It goes rock hard.
One crop per block. Compost it.
